messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Memory Error
parts:
Can anyone confirm the bug I've spend the last few hours dealing with? If you pull the hmc_refactor branch and compile/run the example.stan model, it should call unit_metric_hmc:transition a few times on its own, and then finally call it via the warmup -> run_markov_chain functions. For some reason, when unit_metric_hmc::transition is called in the loop within run_markov_chain, the address of the class instance is changed (but not until after it has returned, as noted by the outputs of "this" at the very beginning and very end of the method).

If you add something like "std::cout << sampler.get_stepsize() << std::endl;" to the beginning of run_markov_chain, before the loop, the problem goes away. This seems it indicate some kind of stack issue, but I can't find any leaks or overflows. I get the same behavior for both clang and g++, which would hopefully indicate that there aren't any compiler errors at play.

If anyone is running Linux, a Valgrind diagnostic would be greatly appreciated.

-Mike

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: Memory Error
parts:
[back on list after I responded to Michael off-list]

On 3/27/13 3:03 PM, Michael Betancourt wrote:
>> Managing this kind of memory-based state of an object
>> is why the STL uses pointer-to-implementation
>> wrappers for classes like std::vector. For std::vector,
>> no matter what the client does (at least in a single threaded
>> environment, the underlying storage array is in a good memory
>> state.
>
> But can this protect against overflow? I think what was happening here was that some other variable was overflowing into the address of a class, so that the class was not pointing to the correct spot in memory anymore. I don't even understand the Boost RNG setup enough to fully understand why it overflowed, but at least it's working now.

Sure -- you just need bounds checking. C++ errs on
the side of speed vs. safety, though, so it's all down
to you.

Boost RNG is pretty straightforward once you understand
what's going to be passed by copy and what's going to
be passed by reference. You absolutely must pass by
reference if you want to share the base RNG --- otherwise
it copies the state, so you wind up with all these highly
correlated RNGs floating around.

>> Of course, C++ is not a "nanny language" like
>> Java, so it happily lets you call methods that are so
>> unsafe they can segfault.
>
> I'm fine with that -- C++ is very much the Spider-Man of languages.

Spidey's powers are elegant. And he's witty.

> With great power comes great responsibility. And memory checkers.

I had no idea Uncle Ben said that in the first Spiderman.
The quote's apparently been around at least since Voltaire.

It's also what JJ Allaire (author of RStudio) said
about C++ when he was here.

- Bob

I just traced through the usage and see the issue
in the base class constructor for HMC samplers:

hmc_base(stan::model::prob_grad& model,
const std::vector<double>& params_r,
const std::vector<int>& params_i,
double epsilon=-1,
double epsilon_pm = 0.0,
bool epsilon_adapt = true,
double delta = 0.651,
double gamma = 0.05,
BaseRNG rand_int = BaseRNG(std::time(0)))
: ...
_rand_uniform_01(_rand_int),
...
{ ... }

The variable rand_int should be passed by non-constant reference.
That means we can't have a default value, which means the order of
params needs to change. We're not using these defaults anywhere, so
no big deal. (You're probably refactoring all this anyway.)

The declarations of the member variables are OK (note the "&"
after the type, which causes the base to be passed by ref
during construction):

boost::uniform_01<BaseRNG&> _rand_uniform_01;

The usages within gm/command.hpp also look OK.

- Bob
